title: Single antimatter particle held and controlled for months
content:
By trapping, cooling, and controlling a single positron for nearly four months, physicists have set the stage for new experiments that can more precisely compare the properties of matter and antimatter

Physicists have trapped and controlled a single positron, the antimatter counterpart of an electron, for months at a time. While positrons have been captured in the past, this is the longest this antimatter particle has been held in a controlled state. The work is aimed at enabling new experiments that can determine whether matter and antimatter are truly mirror images of one another, a question tied to the mystery of why the universe contains so much more matter than antimatter.

Antimatter is a challenge to contain because it transforms into energy if it comes in contact with regular matter. Funded by the U.S. National Science Foundation Mathematical and Physical Sciences Directorate, the achievement allows researchers to measure and control a single particle of antimatter over a long period of time. The advance could enable a key test of the Standard Model of particle physics, the leading theory describing the fundamental particles and forces that govern the universe. The research was conducted at Northwestern University and published in Physical Review Letters.

Antimatter particles have the same mass as their ordinary matter counterparts but otherwise have opposite properties. According to the Standard Model of particle physics, electrons and positrons should have identical properties except for opposite electric charge. Detecting even a tiny difference between the two could indicate the existence of physical phenomena not included in the Standard Model.

To trap antimatter, the team began with fast-moving positrons released by sodium-22, a radioactive form of sodium that naturally emits positrons as it decays. The research team then slowed the speed of the positrons, which are initially traveling at about 87% the speed of light, and cooled them to less than one Kelvin above absolute zero. Using a specialized electromagnetic trap, the researchers then confined a single positron and suspended it in a near-perfect vacuum, preventing it from contacting ordinary matter and annihilating into energy.

Under these highly controlled conditions, the particle behaves like an artificial atom with quantum energy levels that can be precisely manipulated and measured. The team demonstrated that it could drive and detect transitions between those energy levels using carefully tuned microwave signals.

The work builds on decades of research by the team to measure the properties of fundamental particles. In earlier experiments, the team measured a single electron’s magnetic properties with very high accuracy. Their newly demonstrated control of a single positron lays the groundwork for making the same measurement on antimatter. If future measurements reveal that electrons and positrons differ in ways not predicted by the Standard Model, the finding could provide important clues about why the observable universe contains far more matter than antimatter.
